records.title: Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
records.author: pancomplex
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

Main features:

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- MCP support

- Image recognition

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

records.title: Show HN: Cryo – A language whose programs live forever
records.author: zwad3
records.storyText:
Cryo is a programming language that models long-running tasks like workflows or AI agents. Programs freeze to disk when idle and can be thawed when new data arrives.

As part of our announcement of Endothermic Labs, we've put together a small demo of Cryo that highlights its features and walks through the language and its plugin system.

We originally built it as a way to deploy healthcare agents at scale, but have rebuilt it from the ground up to be a standalone toolchain for long-running tasks. It acts as something like a cross between Durable Objects and Temporal workflows, where the script itself is the durable unit with no replay needed.

Cryo is statically and structurally typed, with a concurrency model similar to Go. It's still under active development, so we're holding off on open sourcing it until we're confident that the language is stable, ideally in the next 3-4 weeks.

records.title: Show HN: Markdown is 40× more token-efficient with SQLite
records.author: richardcrng
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Richard, founder of Native. I'm working on open-source context ownership, to stop AI centralisation: https://github.com/withnative/native

My first focus has been making Markdown vaults powerful enough so that teams can self-host all of their context (messaging, docs and projects), without it being externally fragmented or rate-limited.

I'm sharing some early results: Markdown vaults can be 40× more efficient with SQLite!

https://www.withnative.ai/research-and-posts/markdown-contex...

Here's some of the main ideas:

- SQLite or Markdown folders, you pick. You can project the same authoritative event log into either form; more projection formats will follow (e.g. maybe neo4j; we do use a graph structure).

- Empirically: SQLite is better for agents! On a 120 trial evaluation for 11,000 records, agents use 40× fewer tokens with SQLite vs Markdown, per correct answer.

- Everything is a file or SQLite row. Messages, documents and projects: all can be modelled in your vault. You get local-first collaboration with teammates, synced to a cloud of your choice.

- You can render your vault with arbitrary UI. Your WhatsApp-like UI speaks to your teammate's Slack-like UI; both are just views over the same database.

A few things I've learned building this:

- Agents do pretty well even without SQL if you give them strongly typed Markdown frontmatter. This was one arm of the trial I ran. I didn't have any clear expectations, but it was cool to watch: agents ended up writing Python scripts to do SQL-like queries.

- Cumulatively, cached input tokens can get expensive. I feel silly in hindsight here. I'd gotten used to letting my sessions run long, "It's all cached so it's very cheap". But when I looked at my results here, over 2/3 of the token bill on long sessions was cached input...

- "Markdown vaults don't scale as well as databases" isn't as self-evident as I think. This is why I decided to benchmark it... I've had some very blank stares when I try to explain how Markdown files might break at true agent-scale volume.

Unfortunately, the dataset is private, because it's two months of my own work. I am considering open-sourcing it even so, but there is definitely some embarrassing stuff in there. TBD... I know that independent result verification matters!

The core engine that I evaluated is open-source, with more to be released soon: https://github.com/withnative/native

If you're interested in trying connected context on an open engine, you can get updates from our website or email me directly: richard@withnative.ai

https://www.withnative.ai/

records.title: Show HN: Diagonals (Diago) – a chess variation where the pieces stay diagonally
records.author: knarykov
records.storyText:
This is a variation of chess in which, in addition to the arrangement of the pieces, the rules governing pawn movement are altered, and new rules are introduced:

Called Diagonals, Diago, or DiagoChess. Standard 8x8 board. White sets up in the bottom-right corner (King on h1) and moves first; Black sets up in the top-left corner (King on a8).

Movement: Kings, Queens, Rooks, Bishops, and Knights move normally. Pawns move 1 square in any direction to empty squares, but capture strictly diagonally.

Special Rules: No check, checkmate, castling, pawn promotion, or en passant.

Win Conditions: First player to capture the enemy King wins immediately.

Attacked King Mechanics:

Streak Reset: The attacked turn counter resets to zero as soon as your turn starts with your King safe.

You can play this version on the website; I've added full-fledged multiplayer with the ability to create public and private rooms. The multiplayer is powered by NOSTR (nostr relays).

The website features a game against a bot at various difficulty levels, single-screen gameplay, online matches against other players, a time limit like in chess, and even a profile (either as a guest by entering just a nickname, or via Nostr).

records.title: Show HN: Mainplane – Agent in Go that lives on your old PC, drives your laptop
records.author: Alexander9
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Alexander. Yes, this is another agent harness. Here is why I built one anyway.

I was engineer #2 at Browser Use, where I built our agent harness and the evals behind it, including BU Bench, which became a default benchmark for browser agents. I left in September to build Mainplane.

The problem: local agents die with your laptop, and cloud agents can't reach your work. Many cloud platforms ask you to "select a repository", but my work is not that simple. I work across a desktop, a Mac mini and a laptop, and much of it is not in git.

So I loaded Ubuntu on my old 2012 desktop and made it my Mainplane server. It has run for four weeks at a load average of 0.02, because the agents' tools run on other machines.

How it works: it is a control plane architecture. The server runs the harness. It holds your API keys and every session, makes the LLM calls, and routes each tool call to a worker. The workers are your other machines, connected over a built-in private WireGuard network. A bash command runs in the worker's terminal, not on the server. Shared drives let projects move across machines. The agent works on your machines just like you would, but its state lives on the server, and your keys never leave it.

Some design choices:

- Every session is one append-only file. This is the agent state, and it is easily readable. If something breaks, you can resume it from the file. Observability comes for free: agent traces are just these state files.

- Small by design. The system prompt is 3k tokens, and there are just two kinds of tools: shell and file (read, write, edit). At Browser Use, I learned the bitter lesson and found frontier models did better when I deleted all our helper functions. So I made the same bet here: bash is all you need.

- No compaction. When a session fills up, /continue starts a new one that greps the previous state file, retrieving the context it needs, instead of reading a lossy summary. A /compact on a 400k-token session takes a while to write its summary. A /continue into a brand new session starts at once.

- No permission prompts. A hyperintelligent misaligned agent WILL find a way around a permission system. The better strategy is giving the agent full unbounded access to a local computer, and only putting what you trust the agent with on that computer.

- Why Go. WireGuard is written in Go, so the network compiles right into a 20 MB binary. Go is made for production servers, LLMs write it well, and the simplicity of Go matches how I like to build.

Mainplane works with a Claude or ChatGPT subscription on the regular usage limits, or any API key.

I would love your feedback, especially brutal and honest feedback and tasks that the harness cannot do. I'll be here all day to answer questions.

I have been developing a bus communication protocol for a while using the Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040)'s programmable IO (PIO) hardware (basically- 8 tiny processors that run assembly programs to manipulate GPIO pins) and I needed some way of testing my programs, as the real hardware is undebuggable.

Unfortunately, none of the existing emulators I could find supported connecting multiple RP2040s together, and they each had a few different missing bits of functionality, so I decided to make my own!

My emulator supports running multiple RP2040s electrically connected together, and emulates the whole of their PIO blocks (all 8 processors each), along with all of the more niche inter-processor interactions and GPIO functionality I could possibly find in the datasheet.

I built it as a Go package so that it can be used inside of other programs; I intend on using it myself inside a test suite against my in-development protocol.

I've spent quite a long time checking and double-checking most of the logic so it is as complete and accurate as I can make it, but if you spot anything amiss, I'd really appreciate the feedback.

Thanks for checking it out! Hope it can be useful to other RP2040 users.

records.title: Show HN: ssh zydra.sh, a GPU Linux desktop in your terminal, with Doom
records.author: teledream
records.storyText:
ssh zydra.sh

There's no sign-up or anything, and you get a 15-minute demo of a graphical Linux VM drawn entirely in your terminal. It has a browser, an editor, and it runs Doom.

It works best in Kitty or Ghostty. WezTerm and Konsole also work, as well as Sixel and iTerm2 terminals, though with less detail. Text-only terminals support non-graphical apps: shells, editors, and other TUIs.

Why? For a few months I ran coding agents in tmux on a VPS over SSH, and it sucked. I couldn't paste images, scrolling broke and I didn't wanna figure out why, I had no notifications for when an agent finished, I couldn't see browsers agents opened to smoke-test, logins drifted between my laptop and the server, I couldn't check in from my phone, and to know what an agent had done five minutes ago I had to read through opaque chunks of tool calls. These issues added up and had me in a limbo: They made my setup bad enough to annoy me every day, but not quite bad enough to stop my real work and fix it.

How it works: Zydra is a custom (Smithay-based) Wayland compositor in a microVM with an AMD GPU, implementing a series of terminal protocols that solve many issues but are often ignored: Kitty graphics for windows, OSC 52 for the clipboard, images included, OSC 9/99/777 for notifications, SGR mouse for scrolling and clicks. VNC is limited to sending pictures of the screen and diffing frames to find what changed. In Zydra, apps directly tell the compositor what changed, and terminal text is sent as text you can select and copy natively. The browser is a WebKit build that delivers frames to the compositor as DMA-BUFs without a readback, and agents drive it through Playwright. Alt+P is sort of like Raycast: browse apps, linked GitHub, websites, and SSH targets from it.

You can watch the desktop at any point in time and rewind to periodic snapshots. To achieve this, the desktop records into a timeline file, a kind of structured video, and the VM takes snapshots along it. You can traverse back like a livestream to see what happened while you were away, then restore or fork the whole machine from that point. Agents can mark points on the timeline and checkpoint the whole machine before risky changes.

Other things to try:

  ssh -t zydra.sh dino                                           # the Chromium dino game via SSH
  tar -czf - -C ~ .claude .claude.json | ssh -T zydra.sh upload  # bring your configs (includes your Claude login)
  ssh -o ObscureKeystrokeTiming=no -A zydra.sh                   # lower latency & forward your SSH agent
  ssh -p 443 zydra.sh                                            # connect from a corporate firewall
  sshfs zydra.sh: ~/zydra                                        # paid accounts: mount your home
Everything runs on one dedicated server with one AMD iGPU, so there are 12 demo slots. When they're full you wait in a queue and can play Chromium's offline dino game. The paid plan is $40/month (+ tax): 8 GB RAM, 4 vCPUs, 80 GB disk, GPU access, with no time limit and a 3-day money-back guarantee.

I'll be around all day to answer questions.

Hey folks! I made it easier for builders to use the lebanese legislation through: a public DB, API, and MCP.

The Lebanese University has an archive of all laws dating back to 1904 (legallaw.ul.edu.lb). People and AI can barely find it and navigate it. It also had outdated articles.

Now, more people are using it. Builders for their startups, lawyers for their work, and students for their bar prep. I'm still trying to get it trusted by authorities.

The database includes the edges between every law, article, ruling and Gazette issue. You can easily identify how they influence one another.

Articles are versioned, so you can see how it was affected by other laws from the date it was published.

100k unofficial english translations were added using LLMs. They aren't accurate, but they help with search and SEO/AEO/GEO. We're working on producing legally accurate translations.

47k rulings were PDFs, some handwritten. We converted all of them to text using OCR, flagging handwritten files. We're working on an HTR model specifically for those to increase the confidence.

Today, other datasets in Lebanon charge for this data. I'm doing it as a public service. I want change in my country. And, lately, I think it's through helping builders. Yet, what I'm doing is legally wrong, but hopefully morally acceptable.

records.title: Show HN: Gifup – GIF tools that run in the browser (ffmpeg.wasm)
records.author: alexdev2
records.storyText:
Hi HN. GIFUP was an avatar and glitter generator I ran from 2007; it made about 1.3M animations before the web moved on. This year I rebuilt the domain as a set of GIF tools where the encoding happens in the tab via ffmpeg.wasm: video to GIF, compress, resize, crop, captions, GIF to MP4, plus presets that fit Discord, Slack, Twitch and WhatsApp limits.

Nothing is uploaded. The file is read from disk, FFmpeg runs in WebAssembly, and the result is handed back as a blob. The engine is about 10 MB compressed, fetched once and cached. The core is single-threaded because the threaded build needs COOP/COEP headers, so a 10-second 720p clip takes a few seconds rather than a fraction of one. No size caps, no queue, no account.

Two optional server features: "Get a link" hosts a finished file if you want to paste it in a forum, and a WhatsApp sticker page can deliver a sticker to your phone. Both are off until you press the button.

The glue code on the page is plain JS; the FFmpeg build is the unmodified @ffmpeg/core 0.12.6 (GPL, libx264 and libx265 included). I would like to hear where it breaks, especially on Safari, and which tool you are missing.

records.title: Show HN: Sectr – Serverless backend platform for easy deployment of AI agents
records.author: donald_pinckney
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I've been building Sectr, a backend-as-a-service for making it easy(ier) to develop and deploy AI agents. Deploying agents requires non-trivial systems design work. Consider a support agent: how do you stream messages to your frontend, how/where do you persist messages for frontend fetching later (or for auditing), and when the agent wants to issue a refund, do you spin-down the compute infra while it's waiting on human approval? Sectr aims to be the serverless abstraction and platform to provide these systems for you.

No sign-up needed to try using the dev server:

  curl -fsSL https://sectr.dev/install.sh | sh # Install CLI
  sectr init my-agent && cd my-agent # Starter code
  sectr dev # Dev server, with UI to test chatting
Sectr provides:

- Streaming of every token, tool call and event, and persistence so they can be loaded fresh later.

- Scaling up, and down to zero when the agent needs to wait, and resumption right to the suspended agent's state.

- Human approved tools automatically use Sectr's suspension and resumption capabilities, no code needed from you.

- AG-UI endpoint for any deployed agent so you can trivially hook up your frontend

- Local dev server experience, so you can rapidly debug and iterate on your agent's behavior

At the core, you can deploy any container image to Sectr as long as it implements a certain shaped HTTP endpoint. In practice, currently Sectr provides adapters to let you deploy your existing OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, or Pydantic AI agents, with only 2 new lines of code:

  app = AgentApp(name="support")
  app.add_route("/chat", openai_agents(agent))
Certainly the hardest part of building Sectr was getting the resumption logic to be correct and invisible, across the Program State x Model Provider x Agent Framework matrix. For example, an earlier bug was when a model replied with text plus a tool call, Sectr would resume that as two separate messages, instead of one message with a text and tool part. This works, but breaks prompt caching (and might subtly change model behavior).

Sectr is free during the beta (and can be tried locally without sign-up); I mainly want feedback, especially on dev & deployment experiences, any bugs, and what features would excite you.

Introductory video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-y3wynkKc0

Docs: https://docs.sectr.dev

records.title: Show HN: Limma – MCP for total recall and precision in data retrieval for agents
records.author: BerendG
records.storyText:
Hello, my name is Berend Graham. My cofounder Shiv Oberai and I have been working on Limma for a year now with the goal of building a proactive solution to the reliability issues that plague practical AI and agentic use in companies with RAG.

Limma is a single MCP that exists for the sole purpose of ensuring that the right information is retrieved with every query and no information is skipped and or missed. This means total precision and recall. We've found that this approach leads to the lowest rate of hallucination vs. solely targeting agent action verification which has made tremendous strides in capability.

We do this by building a map and structuring all data-points within unstructured data as well as federating structured data for addressability so that agents don't need to search through chunks directly and instead only get the right information . We wanted this to be extremely easy to use so that anyone can set it up and try it within minutes so that the precision issues (especially with large quantities of data) that LLMs struggle with can finally be remedied. We use self-hosted models (primarily Qwen models as of current) so that the system can be deployed on one's own server if needed, and also to optimize for speed.

We have a free monthly version on our website if anyone would like to try it out and provide feedback!

records.author: sam256
records.storyText:
This is hardly a greenfield area. There are tons of agent-to-agent communication apps. But, at least to my taste, a lot of them are too complicated or too opinionated. If we learned anything from the HuggingFace incident, it's that modern AI agents don't need a lot of help communicating. They are smart and creative and figure it out.

So...with that in mind, I (meaning I + claude and friends) built kashkeshet, or kkt. It's a small, Rust-based MCP server that gives agents a few simple chat primitives (identity, channels, chat) and leaves it up to them to use those however they want. You as the human get a little web interface so you can watch the fun.

Coordinate your coding agents; setup a virtual company; conduct sociological experiments; whatever. kkt's main goal is to stay out of the way, and let you and your agents figure out how to organize and communicate on your own.

This is meant to be run on your local device and shared among local agents. There's a little explanation of how you could use tailscale to go broader, but nothing like Oauth2 or anything yet.

records.title: Show HN: Flowfile – Open-source visual ETL that round-trips to Python (Polars)
records.author: edwardeechoud
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Edward, the author of Flowfile.

Flowfile is a visual ETL tool built on Polars. You build pipelines on a canvas, and every flow is also Python code. You can export it or write code with the FlowFrame API (Polars-like) and it shows up as a visual graph (or vice versa - keep reading).

Flowfile is what it is today because I believe we are spending too much time translating non-technical and technical implementations of data problems. Sometimes visual works better, and sometimes code. You should be able to choose whichever is easiest, without fully committing to one way of working. Flowfile solves this by standardizing the backend component without favoring either visual or code.

Which brings me to Flowfile's newest feature: notebook mode. The flow opens as Python cells that stay in sync with the canvas. If you add a filter (df.filter(...)) in a cell, it appears on the canvas. And it also works the other way around: if you add a sort on the canvas, it appears as a .sort(...) in the notebook. So now you can switch between visual and code without making a total mess of it under the hood.

It also has a data catalog, a scheduler, sandboxed Python execution, etc.. It's MIT licensed, and `pip install flowfile` installs all dependencies.

Github: https://github.com/edwardvaneechoud/Flowfile

I'd love feedback, especially on the notebook mode.

records.title: Show HN: Snippet – an always-on AI agent
records.author: snipextt
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I built an always on always listening AI Agent, here's some backstory:

I've always struggled with the attention problem while developing. Even with agents, I can work fast, but I don't know if I can keep working for long, or if I can come back to a problem once I get distracted. So a little while ago I built Snippet for myself.

It's an always-on, code-first agent based on my own struggles with writing code. It tracks, it remembers, it speaks and it listens. Always on, unless my battery dies and I forget to plug in my charger. When I step away, it holds my place, and when I come back the work is still there, waiting, right where I left it.

I believe for agents to be anything more than they are, they need to be aware of the physical world, of what's going on. I'm still finding efficient ways to build that in, and this is an early demo.

A heads-up: a large part of the codebase is AI-generated. I'm in the middle of a lot of refactoring and developing. It works and it's efficient, but expect some rough edges.

I'd love honest feedback on the idea. If you can, please try it and tell me what you think. There are apps across different platforms for testing it, and I've linked them below.

records.title: Show HN: Model Salt, fixing the pelican problem in LLMs by adding entropy
records.author: Benjaminsen
records.storyText:
I have been frustrated with how repetitive the output of LLMs is. Even at maximum temperature, asking the same prompt ten times gives functionally the same result each time, as discussed here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50090443

That’s not surprising considering how LLMs work, but the thread above got me wondering if you could push models away from their usual generation patterns by injecting entropy from an external source.

After a lot of tweaking and experimenting, I turned the idea into an MCP server. It's optimized to add just enough entropy that creative output stops being repetitive, while still living up to the intent of the original prompt.

I’d love feedback, particularly on the approach itself. If you have a better way to inject entropy than what I have found, a pull request is very welcome: https://github.com/modelsalt/model-salt

records.storyText:
I built something for someone who needed a website, but didn't want to be exposed to yet another complicated CMS like WordPress. They already use Google Docs, so I built Foldocs for them to publish and maintain a simple website.

Foldocs creates static HTML pages out of a (shared) folder of documents in Google Drive (or Nextcloud!): (sub)folders become (sub)sections on the site, and documents inside them become pages. Does it work? Proof is to be found in the pudding: Foldocs.com, the site that explains Foldocs, is itself a Foldocs site! The underlying Google Drive is here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ZRYhiIGfSeIcA_gjRVgT....

Foldocs is an open source (AGPL 3.0) Python engine anyone can run. It currently supports three themes, dark mode, and an RSS feed. You can also try it out by creating a preview on https://try.foldocs.com. Paste a shared folder link, and see a preview (kept for 7 days, limited in files / size, and only syncs manually). Previews are running on a separate domain and a throwaway VPS, since hosting strangers' content on the internet is... scary.

Curious to hear what you think of the concept, learn what breaks (but don't try too hard please), what you run into, and/or what is missing!

records.title: Show HN: Play ten years of stock picking in an evening, on a simulated market
records.author: whatever_works
records.storyText:
This is a stock picking game that simulates a stock market with thousands of rule based agents making trades and moving the stock price. The agents (not AI agents) have different rules to simulate different trading styles. The game layer is basically 12 companies/stocks you can buy and sell, and a clock you can advance on your own time. So you can play 10 years in one sitting, and see the results of your "long term thinking" and decision making. You can challenge friends to see who can get the highest return in 1 year or 10 years or whatever.

Would love to hear any feedback!

records.title: Show HN: pw-repl - A Playwright-powered REPL for you and your agents to share
records.author: arcanemachiner
records.storyText:
For the busy people out there, the GitHub repo has a demo video so you can see if this is worth your time: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

The video was created by Opus 5.5; I just asked it to create a demo video (it has a 'record' tool), so I think this is a good idea of how well it can work with the tool.

---

pw-repl is a tool that makes it easy for you and your agents to work with Playwright+CDP in a browser (your current headed session, or a headless one, or both at the same time; take your pick).

It's basically a Playwright-powered swiss army knife that helps you and agents poke around your browser: Try out different features of a website, break things (e.g. mock backend responses), take screenshots, record videos, etc.

The GitHub repo shows a video, recorded by an agent using pw-repl: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

One cool thing it can do: create videos of bug reports. You can tell an agent about a bug and to use pw-repl to capture it, and it can record a video with the built-in toast feature to narrate its actions, and show a virtual mouse to simulate actions on the screen, as if it were a user. It's also useful for capturing screenshots (which can be combined with the toast and highlight tools to emphasize certain elements or information), and has many useful features that can help agents to use it efficiently.

This isn't intended to be commercialized in any way. It's just a neat tool that I (with Claude's help) cobbled together. It's completely vibe-coded, and is intended mainly as a debugging aid. I use all the time, and hope it may be helpful for others.

It's basically just Playwright + CDP under the hood, but has some extra tools and an interface that make it easier for agents to work with.

The quickest way to try it out is to tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background --launch`, which starts a headless Chromium of its own. No browser setup needed. (If you don't like such `curl | bash`-esque installation instructions, read the code, or get your agent to take a look at it.)

To use it in your own browser instead, start Chrome with CDP enabled (`chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/chrome-debug"`), and tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background`. (The separate `--user-data-dir` is needed because recent versions of Chrome don't open the debugging port on your default profile.)

It also can generate a skill so that you can just run `/pw-repl do some stuff`. Get your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest skill > <skills folder>/pw-repl/SKILL.md` (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/pw-repl/SKILL.md` for Claude Code).

NOTE: This has only been tested on my Linux machine, so not sure if it will work on macOS. It should, but I haven't tried it out personally.

Fun fact: This tool was originally a random REPL that Claude generated on-the-fly to do some random thing. I saw it and was blown away, so I got Claude to make it into its own application. I suspect that Claude may have taken "inspiration" from an existing project with a similar name, so credit where credit is due to this other `playwright-repl` package: https://github.com/stevez/playwright-repl
